pp-1001.clientCommunication: Thanks for sending photos and details about your dog's itching. It sounds like her skin flares up seasonally, and the rusty color between her toes is often just saliva staining from licking rather than a separate problem. We'd like to see her for an exam and some simple in-house skin tests to check for secondary infection or irritation and make sure her flea prevention is fully on track. In the meantime, please try to avoid any new soaps or lotions on her skin and keep up her flea/tick medication consistently, and let us know if she starts scratching more intensely, seems uncomfortable, or you notice any sores or odor.

Clinical picture is consistent with pyotraumatic dermatitis (hot spot), likely triggered by moisture retention in the dense coat and self-trauma from scratching or head shaking. Head shaking raises concern for concurrent otitis externa as an underlying pruritic trigger. No systemic signs (lethargy, anorexia, fever) reported by owner.

These can be quite uncomfortable, so please try to prevent him from further scratching or rubbing the area (an e-collar can help) until we can see him. We'd also like to check his ears since the head shaking could be a related issue. Please bring him in within the next day or two so we can clean the area, check for infection, and get him comfortable.

triage.rationale: History strongly suggests dermatophytosis (ringworm) with likely zoonotic transmission to a child; needs prompt confirmation and treatment to limit further spread.

A recently introduced kitten in the household has a similar lesion, and a human household member has developed an annular pruritic lesion, a pattern highly suggestive of dermatophytosis. No systemic signs (lethargy, inappetence, vomiting) are reported. Physical exam, Wood's lamp screening, and fungal culture/PCR are needed to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment and decontamination.

pp-1003.clientCommunication: Thank you for the detailed history — the pattern you're describing, especially with your new kitten having a similar patch and your daughter developing an itchy ring on her arm, makes us want to check your cat for a common fungal skin infection that can pass between pets and people. It's very treatable once confirmed, but we'd like to see your cat soon so we can run a couple of simple tests and get treatment started for all the pets in the home. In the meantime, try to limit close contact between the animals and family members, wash hands after handling either pet, and it would be a good idea to have your daughter's skin lesion checked by her pediatrician. We'll have a clearer picture after the exam and test results.

triage.rationale: A rapidly growing, fluctuating, red lump in a Boxer is suspicious for a mast cell tumor, which needs prompt sampling before any manipulation or removal.

Boxers are a breed strongly predisposed to mast cell tumors, which can present exactly this way. No systemic signs (vomiting, inappetence, lethargy) are reported by the owner, but these should be specifically screened for at the visit. Prior history of benign lipomas does not rule out a new, biologically distinct mass.

The combination of anuria, vomiting, and lethargy in this signalment raises strong concern for urethral obstruction with possible early post-renal azotemia and hyperkalemia. This is a time-critical presentation requiring immediate physical exam (bladder palpation) and stabilization.
